lines.caption: This is a tour of pull request 70, which runs fewer CI jobs and edits CI's PR comments less often.
lines.say: This is a tour of pull request seventy, which runs fewer CI jobs and edits CI's PR comments less often.

lines.caption: It has three parts: what the PR adds, how it was built and verified, and what comes later.
Part 1. What this PR adds.
The release folded into verify, the report job run only for a fix, and unchanged comments left alone.
On a PR, the review job now writes its own comment, unless it has a fix to push.
When a comment's new text is the same as the old, CI skips the edit, so nobody is woken.
A screenshot audit comment now updates the summary directly, instead of re-running a job.
The PR still shows the same checks; the report job is simply skipped when there's no fix.
On a push to main, build and verify run as before.
The release is now published at the end of the verify job.
So a release now goes out only once its packages passed the tests.
Actions ran out of minutes on 7 November, partly because GitHub rounds every short job up to a whole minute.
lines.say: Actions ran out of minutes on the seventh of November, partly because GitHub rounds every short job up to a whole minute.

lines.caption: So folding a ten-second job into one that already runs saves a whole billed minute.
Most reviews leave no fix, so the review job posts its findings itself, from a fresh checkout, without the push token.
A fix still goes to the separate report job, so the model never shares a machine with the token.
The comment script reads the comment first, and skips the edit when the new body is identical.
The summary workflow now runs the summary script itself, once the head's build run has finished.
The changes step, the no-code markers and ccache all stay, and the merge rule allows the skipped report job.
Build is unchanged: it stamps the release version and builds the packages.
Verify is unchanged too: it installs them and runs every test.
The release steps run at the end of verify, which could already write to the repo, so build stays read-only.
Before, the release needed only a build; now failing tests hold it back.
Issue 58 wanted a merge to release the PR's own packages, stamped with the next version.
lines.say: Issue fifty-eight wanted a merge to release the PR's own packages, stamped with the next version.

lines.caption: But every open PR would then carry that version, and a test install could block the real release.
Re-stamping packages at release time isn't clean, so that issue stays open.
The PR changes the two workflows, three CI scripts, the digest agent and the merge rule, plus this page.
To undo it, revert the PR. If a flaky test holds a release back, re-run the failed jobs.
Part 2. How it was built and verified.
It was built from the jobs it folds and checked by a fresh review and this PR's own CI run. Thunar's code doesn't change.
The report job stays as it was for a fix; its report command also runs inside the review job.
The release steps use the same two scripts, unchanged, beside verify's existing write access.
And the summary script already ran from any job, so the summary workflow calls it the same way.
Both workflows and every script were checked for syntax in the building session.
On this PR's first CI run, the review wrote its own report, and the report job was skipped.
A stub test showed an unchanged comment isn't edited, and a changed one is edited once.
That run billed five jobs where pull request 69's last run billed six.
A fresh review found seven issues in the first version; both serious ones are fixed.
The first version ran the report beside the model, which could have left files or a process to steal the token.
And a fork's build cache could have reached a release, which became moot once issue 58 was left out.
CI's own review found nine; six are fixed in one push, and three wait on the owner.
Its second review found six more; the confirmed one, scripts run from an edited tree, is fixed, and three small ones accepted.
The third review passed; three more small fixes went in, one cost was accepted, and one question went to the owner.
The fourth review passed; the report job now also covers a failed checkout, and one small finding was accepted.
The fifth review found that fallback still wrong, so one explicit output now hands the report over.
The sixth review found three edge cases in that hand-over, and all three are fixed.
The seventh review passed; four small fixes went in, and three small findings were accepted.
The release from verify first runs when this PR merges.
The summary workflow's new path first runs on the next audit after the merge.
Part 3. What comes later.
No open issue depends on this one; issue 58 stays open for a cleaner answer.
lines.say: No open issue depends on this one; issue fifty-eight stays open for a cleaner answer.

lines.caption: After pull request 69 and this one, reusing a merged PR's packages is what's left.
lines.say: After pull request sixty-nine and this one, reusing a merged PR's packages is what's left.

lines.caption: After the merge, its own run should publish the release from verify.
The explainer job stays separate, since its check is part of the merge rule.
In short: fewer billed jobs and quieter PR comments, with releases only after tests pass.
